# Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results {.unnumbered} The day ends with two checks on the analysis and its report, then a README assembled from everything your repository now holds. Each part splits the work the same way: | You own | The AI writes | The independent check | |---|---|---| | The original code and its output | A translation | Do both versions give the same output? | | The numbers in your report | Text around inline code | Is any number typed rather than computed? | | The codebook, lockfile, scripts and AI-use log | A README drafted from them | Can every statement be traced to one of those files? | You check the agent's work from the R console and the Git pane, as in [checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work). Two more statistical checks (robustness and simulation) are in *Going further*. *⏱ ~30 minutes* ## Part A: Translation with an equivalence check *⏱ ~15 minutes* AI translates code quickly: base R to tidyverse, or SPSS, Stata or SAS to R. An equivalence checkA comparison showing that two versions of code, such as an original and an AI translation, give the same output once only presentation (types, row order) is normalised. runs both versions and compares the outputs, as in [Block 9](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd). The agent writes the translation; the shipped `tests/test_translation.R`, which it did not write, decides whether it is equivalent. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Translate and compare (15 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Start:** your workshop repository, committed and clean, with Claude Code in Manual mode (`default`) in the Terminal tab, which the repository sets. **1. Run the original.** In the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(here) voles <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"), stringsAsFactors = TRUE) rate_mean <- aggregate(metabolic_rate_post ~ treatment_arm + sex, data = voles, FUN = mean) rate_n <- aggregate(metabolic_rate_post ~ treatment_arm + sex, data = voles, FUN = length) names(rate_n)[3] <- "n" legacy_summary <- merge(rate_mean, rate_n, by = c("treatment_arm", "sex")) legacy_summary ``` ::: **2. Ask for a translation.** **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Translate this base R code into a tidyverse function summarise_rate_tidy(data) in scripts/functions/summaries.R. It takes the tibble returned by load_voles() and returns one row per treatment_arm and sex, with the columns treatment_arm, sex, metabolic_rate_post (the mean) and n. Use the native pipe. Do not edit any other file. [paste the base R code from step 1] ``` Approve the edit when asked, after reading it. **3. Compare.** Normalise only *presentation* (type and row order), never values; `waldo::compare()` shows what still differs. In the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R")) source(here("scripts", "functions", "summaries.R")) tidy_summary <- summarise_rate_tidy(load_voles()) normalise <- function(data) { data |> as_tibble() |> mutate(across(where(is.factor), as.character)) |> arrange(treatment_arm, sex) } waldo::compare(normalise(tidy_summary), normalise(legacy_summary)) ``` ::: **4. Find the difference.** A different column name is presentation: ask for a rename. A different value is behaviour: find out why before reading on. No difference? Check how the translation handled the missing value anyway.
`aggregate()` with a formula silently drops rows with a missing value, so the animal with no `metabolic_rate_post` is left out of both the mean and the count. A direct translation with `summarise(mean(metabolic_rate_post), n())` returns `NA` for that cell and counts the animal in `n`. Neither is "the translation": they make different decisions about missing data. Decide which you want, write it explicitly (`na.rm = TRUE` and a count of non-missing values), and record the decision. It is Block 9's "unchanged is not correct", from a different direction.
**5. Run the shipped test.** Restart R (*Session → Restart R*), then in the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_translation.R")) ``` ::: The test uses the original code as its reference. If you chose different missing-value handling, it fails, correctly: change the test's reference and say why in your commit message. **6. Log it and commit.** Add a line to `docs/ai-log.md`, for example: ``` 2026-10-19; Claude Code (model as shown above the Claude Code prompt); translated summary script to tidyverse; kept the translation, matched the original's missing-value handling after the equivalence check ``` Then commit `summaries.R` and the log from the Git pane, with a message that records the missing-value decision. **You are done when** `test_translation.R` passes in a fresh R session and your commit message records how missing values are handled. **If it goes wrong:** if the agent edited anything other than `summaries.R`, select the file in the Git pane and choose **Revert**. If you run short of time, write `summarise_rate_tidy()` yourself from the hidden explanation above. :::: ::: From other software, export the original's results to a file and compare against those. Expect differences in defaults (missing values, quantiles, rounding); each needs a decision, not a looser tolerance. ## Part B: Reporting without typed numbers *⏱ ~7 minutes* A typed number can be mistyped, or go stale when the data change, and an assistant drafting text may restate numbers it saw earlier. So every number in the prose comes from inline code. In a code chunk of your report: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # fit the pre-registered primary analysis library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R")) voles_df <- load_voles() |> mutate(treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"))) fit <- lm(mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, data = voles_df) ci <- confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ] primary <- tibble( estimate = unname(coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]), lower = unname(ci[1]), upper = unname(ci[2]) ) ``` ::: and in the text of the report: ``` High-dose voles were `r round(primary$estimate, 2)` g heavier than controls after treatment (95% CI `r round(primary$lower, 2)` to `r round(primary$upper, 2)` g). ``` Your `AGENTS.md` asks for this; the shipped `find_typed_numbers()` checks it, by listing prose lines that still contain numbers outside inline code. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## `scripts/functions/typed_numbers.R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/typed_numbers.R ---- # List the prose lines of a .qmd file that still contain numbers outside # inline code, for you to review by eye. Years, design sizes and YAML values # are flagged too, so treat each hit as a question, not an error. find_typed_numbers <- function(path) { lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE) is_fence <- grepl("^```", lines) in_chunk <- cumsum(is_fence) %% 2 == 1 tibble::tibble(line = seq_along(lines), text = lines) |> dplyr::filter(!in_chunk, !is_fence) |> dplyr::mutate(prose = gsub("`\\{?r\\}? [^`]*`", "", text)) |> dplyr::filter(grepl("[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+|\\b[0-9]{2,}\\b", prose, perl = TRUE)) |> dplyr::select(line, text) } ``` ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Scan a report (3 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Start:** the template's `reports/example_report.qmd`, an interim summary of the voles trial with some numbers typed in. **1. Scan it.** In the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "typed_numbers.R")) find_typed_numbers(here::here("reports", "example_report.qmd")) |> print(n = Inf, width = Inf) ``` ::: **2. Sort the hits.** The scan flags five lines. Decide for each one whether it is a typed result that should be inline code, or a number that is fine as text.
Lines 37 and 38 are typed results (the 1.53 g difference with its interval, and the mean of 29.4 g): both should be inline code. The other three can stay: the date in the YAML header (line 3), the design size of 12 per group (line 28), and "95%" in "95% CI" (line 34).
**You are done when** you can say which two lines are typed results and why the other three can stay. **If it goes wrong:** if `find_typed_numbers()` is not found, check that the `source()` line ran without an error. :::: ::: The same scan works on any `.qmd` you write, including your Quarto report from Day 3. Every hit is a question, not an error. ## Part C: The repository you leave with *⏱ ~8 minutes* Your repository now holds most of what a reader needs: a codebookA table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI., cleaning logs, numbered scripts, a lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment., tests and an AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.. A README pulls them together. The rule: the AI may only phrase facts you can trace to a file; anything else becomes a visible placeholder for you to fill. ::::::: {.dia .dia-flow role="figure" aria-label="The README is drafted by the AI only from four kinds of file in your repository: the codebook and data note, the numbered scripts, renv.lock and the AI-use log. You then trace every statement back to a file."} :::::: {.dia-branches} ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `docs/codebook.csv`, `docs/data_note.md` ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} numbered scripts in `scripts/` ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `renv.lock` ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `docs/ai-log.md` ::: :::::: ::: {.dia-arrow} the only sources ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Drafts `README.md`, with placeholders for anything missing ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} You trace every statement to a file ::: ::::::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Draft from the record, then audit (8 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Start:** your workshop repository, committed and clean. If Block 7 or 9 is unfinished, switch to the `block9-done` branch from the Git pane's branch menu first, so the files the README draws on exist. **1. Run the whole suite first.** Restart R (*Session → Restart R*), then in the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} renv::status() callr::r(\(d) testthat::test_dir(d), list(here::here("tests"))) ``` ::: `renv::status()` should report no problems, and the tests should run with no failures (the README test still skips). This is the evidence the README's "How to verify" section will point to. **2. Draft.** In Claude Code, in Manual mode (`default`): **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Create or update README.md for this repository. Use ONLY these sources, and name the source of each section: - Data: docs/codebook.csv and docs/data_note.md. - Scripts and run order: the numeric prefixes of the files in scripts/. - Dependencies: the R version and packages pinned in renv.lock, and the restore command renv::restore(). - How to verify: the command callr::r(\(d) testthat::test_dir(d), list(here::here("tests"))), and what the tests check. - AI declaration: a summary of docs/ai-log.md, making no claim beyond it. Where a value is not in these files (authors, ORCIDs, licence, DOI, funding, units the codebook leaves blank), insert a visible placeholder in exactly this form: **TODO: supply [field]: not provided** Edit README.md only. Show me your plan first. ``` **3. Let the test audit it.** The shipped `tests/test_readme.R` checks the README against its sources: the R and package versions against `renv.lock`, every numbered script, no leftover `{{` tokens, and no invented unit for `metabolic_rate_post`. In the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_readme.R")) ``` ::: It also reports how many placeholders are left. Then trace one statement the test cannot check by hand: confirm that the AI declarationA statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded. says no more than your log. **4. Confirm the scope.** The Git pane should show only `README.md` as changed. **5. Before you share it.** The placeholders are your to-do list. Work through licence, ORCIDs, DOI and archiving with the [SORTEE checklist from Day 2](06-reproducibility.qmd#repro-sortee). Then add the last line to `docs/ai-log.md`, and commit. **6. Payoff.** What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again? **You are done when** `test_readme.R` passes and the whole suite passes in a fresh R session. **If it goes wrong:** if the agent changed any file other than `README.md`, select it in the Git pane and choose **Revert**. If the README test fails, ask Claude Code to fix only the statements the test names, and run it again. :::: ::: A fuller version, with a README skill, is in *Going further* in [Block 8](11h-code-review.qmd). Check your institution's and target journal's policy on declaring AI use. :::{.callout-note} ## Check · Reproduce · Record - **You can now:** have an agent translate analysis code and draft a README, **trusted because** shipped tests compare the translation with the original and the README with its sources, and the whole suite passes in a fresh R session. - **Check:** an equivalence test between the original and the translation; a scan for typed numbers; every README statement traced to a file. - **Reproduce:** numbers come from code, so the report updates when the data do; the README's dependencies come from `renv.lock`, not from memory. - **Record:** the README and the AI-use log complete the record. Together with the codebook, logs, tests and lockfile, they are what a reviewer, a co-author or you in a year's time will need. ::: ## Check your understanding **A translated script and the original disagree only after you convert factors to characters and sort the rows. What should you do next?**
**The README draft gives the unit of `metabolic_rate_post`, but your codebook leaves it blank. What should you do?**
## Going further (not covered live) This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. ### Robustness, not choice AI should not choose your primary analysis. The BLADE benchmark compared language-model agents with expert analysts on open-ended research questions. It found that the models were often limited to basic analyses, and that agents able to explore the data made more varied but still sub-optimal analytical decisions (Gu et al., 2024). Its useful role is narrower: listing defensible alternatives to an analysis you have already fixed, so you can check whether your conclusion depends on the choice. Run the steps yourself, and judge each answer before running it. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Enumerate, judge, run :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Ask for alternatives, not a recommendation:** ``` My pre-registered primary analysis is an ANCOVA: mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, estimating the High_dose versus Control difference. List alternative specifications a reasonable analyst might use for the same question, and for each, say whether it estimates the same quantity. Do not recommend one. ``` **2. Judge each one yourself.** Mark each alternative defensible or not, with a reason. Check especially whether it estimates the *same* quantity. **3. Run the defensible ones** and report them beside the primary analysis. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R")) voles_df <- load_voles() |> mutate(treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"))) specs_df <- tribble( ~spec, ~formula, "Primary: ANCOVA", "mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex", "Change score", "I(mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) ~ treatment_arm + sex", "ANCOVA with arm-by-sex", "mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm * sex" ) spec_results_df <- specs_df |> mutate(result = map(formula, \(f) { fit <- lm(as.formula(f), data = voles_df) ci <- confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ] tibble( estimate = unname(coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]), lower = unname(ci[1]), upper = unname(ci[2]) ) })) |> unnest(result) spec_results_df ``` :::
In the third specification, the coefficient `treatment_armHigh_dose` is the High_dose effect **in females only** (the reference level of `sex`), because the model includes an interaction. It sits in the same column as the other estimates but answers a different question. It belongs in a separate analysis of whether the effect differs by sex, not in a table of estimates of the same quantity. An AI that lists it as an "alternative" without saying so has made exactly the error step 2 asks you to catch.
:::: ::: :::{.callout-warning} Running many specifications and reporting the one you like best is selective reporting. The primary analysis is fixed in advance; the others are reported as sensitivity analyses whatever they show. ::: #### Check your understanding: robustness **Why should the arm-by-sex interaction model not appear in the same robustness table as the primary ANCOVA?**
### Simulation and parameter recovery If you simulate data from a mechanism whose parameters you chose, a correct analysis should recover those parameters on average, and its 95% confidence intervals should contain the true values about 95% of the time. This tests the analysis code against a known answer, which real data never provide. Morris, White and Crowther (2019) give a structure for planning simulation studies: the **aims**, the **data-generating mechanism**, the **estimand**, the **methods** and the **performance measures** (ADEMP). Here: - **Aim:** check that the analysis code estimates the high-dose effect correctly. - **Data-generating mechanism:** 12 voles per arm-by-sex cell. Pre-treatment mass is normal with mean 28 g and SD 2 g. Post-treatment mass equals 2.8 g plus 0.9 times pre-treatment mass, plus 0.8 g for Low_dose, plus 1.5 g for High_dose, plus 1.0 g for males, plus normal error with SD 0.8 g. - **Estimand:** the difference in post-treatment mass between High_dose and Control, adjusted for pre-treatment mass and sex. True value: 1.5 g. - **Method:** linear model (ANCOVA), `mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex`. - **Performance measures:** bias and confidence-interval coverage, each with its Monte Carlo standard error. The written mechanism is yours. It is the equivalent of the codebook in [Block 7](11g-data-cleaning.qmd): the AI turns it into code, and you check the code against it. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Write, check, recover :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Simulation code.** Give the AI the data-generating mechanism above, word for word, and ask for a function `simulate_voles()` returning a tibble with columns `treatment_arm`, `sex`, `mass_pre_g` and `mass_post_g`. **2. Check the simulated data against the specification.** Before using the function, run it once and check that it matches what you wrote: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1) sim_df <- simulate_voles() sim_df |> count(treatment_arm, sex) # 12 per cell? sim_df |> summarise(mean(mass_pre_g), sd(mass_pre_g)) sim_df |> summarise(mean_post = mean(mass_post_g), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex)) ``` ::: High_dose should be about 1.5 g above Control within each sex, and males about 1 g above females. If not, the simulation is wrong, and nothing built on it can be trusted. **3. Analysis code, in a separate session.** Without showing it the simulation code, ask the AI for a function `estimate_high_vs_control(data)` that fits the model above and returns the High_dose estimate and its 95% confidence interval. **4. Run the recovery.**
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} simulate_voles <- function(n_per_cell = 12, effect_low = 0.8, effect_high = 1.5, sex_effect = 1.0, slope_pre = 0.9, sd_pre = 2, sd_resid = 0.8) { tidyr::expand_grid( treatment_arm = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"), sex = c("F", "M"), animal = seq_len(n_per_cell) ) |> dplyr::mutate( mass_pre_g = stats::rnorm(dplyr::n(), mean = 28, sd = sd_pre), arm_effect = dplyr::case_when( treatment_arm == "Low_dose" ~ effect_low, treatment_arm == "High_dose" ~ effect_high, .default = 0 ), mass_post_g = 28 * (1 - slope_pre) + slope_pre * mass_pre_g + arm_effect + sex_effect * (sex == "M") + stats::rnorm(dplyr::n(), sd = sd_resid) ) |> dplyr::select(treatment_arm, sex, mass_pre_g, mass_post_g) } estimate_high_vs_control <- function(data) { data <- dplyr::mutate( data, treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")) ) fit <- stats::lm(mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, data = data) ci <- stats::confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ] tibble::tibble( estimate = unname(stats::coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]), lower = unname(ci[1]), upper = unname(ci[2]) ) } ``` :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) n_sim <- 1000 true_effect <- 1.5 results_df <- seq_len(n_sim) |> map(\(i) estimate_high_vs_control(simulate_voles(effect_high = true_effect))) |> list_rbind() results_df |> summarise( bias = mean(estimate) - true_effect, bias_mcse = sd(estimate) / sqrt(n_sim), coverage = mean(lower <= true_effect & upper >= true_effect), coverage_mcse = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / n_sim), empirical_se = sd(estimate) ) ``` ::: Bias should be within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of zero. Coverage should be within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of 0.95, roughly 0.936 to 0.964 with 1,000 runs. **5. Prove the check can fail.** Replace the analysis with a version that models the change the wrong way round, as in [Block 3](11c-debugging.qmd): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_buggy <- function(data) { data <- dplyr::mutate( data, treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")), mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g ) fit <- stats::lm(mass_change_g ~ treatment_arm + sex, data = data) ci <- stats::confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ] tibble::tibble( estimate = unname(stats::coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]), lower = unname(ci[1]), upper = unname(ci[2]) ) } ``` ::: Rerun the recovery with `estimate_buggy()`. Bias should be about −3 g and coverage near zero. A check you have never seen fail is a check you are assuming works. :::: ::: :::{.callout-warning} **What recovery does not prove.** It shows that the code estimates the right quantity *under the mechanism you simulated*. It says nothing about whether real voles behave like that. A change-score model fitted to these simulated data would also be nearly unbiased (randomisation makes both estimators valid), but less precise; compare `empirical_se` to see the cost. Recovery tests code, not scientific assumptions. ::: #### Check your understanding: simulation **A simulation recovers the true effect with negligible bias and 95% coverage. What has it shown?**
## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
AI-use log A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.
AI declaration A statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded.
codebook A table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI.
equivalence check A comparison showing that two versions of code, such as an original and an AI translation, give the same output once only presentation (types, row order) is normalised.
lockfile The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.
````` ::: ::: ## References - Gu, K., Shang, R., Jiang, R., et al. (2024). BLADE: Benchmarking language model agents for data-driven science. In *Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024*, 13936–13971. - Morris, T.P., White, I.R. and Crowther, M.J. (2019).
